stories.headline: Update: Parties Make Final Appeals on Eve of Midterms as Democrats Eye Senate; Michigan Race Upended by Stevens Endorsement
stories.summary:
With one day before the midterm elections, both parties are delivering closing arguments. Democrats appear within striking distance of a Senate majority, though many contested seats are toss-ups in Republican-leaning states. Decision Desk HQ forecasts Democratic flips in Texas, Alaska and Maine. A new NBC News poll put President Trump's disapproval at a record 60 percent, with Democrats holding a 7-point lead, and a New York Times/Siena survey showed Democratic Senate candidates ahead in seven battleground states.

President Trump planned a closing address Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he is expected to promote his Washington beautification projects and the agenda advanced by Republicans since the start of his second term. At Iowa rallies he predicted Republican sweeps, saying voters would elect "America first" Republicans. In a Fox News clip, he said he might become "Mr. Veto" if Democrats win a chamber. Critics noted that he chose a Washington event over travel to battleground states; supporters said it showcases his record.

In Michigan, Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed after a dispute over an outside ad she called antisemitic. El-Sayed said "none of this matters" and is focused on the cost of living. Democrats including Neera Tanden condemned the move, while Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson welcomed Stevens to the GOP. The Times/Siena poll, taken before the endorsement, showed El-Sayed leading by 11 points.

Legal fights are also in focus. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department suit seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses; the administration said it would appeal. Polls and forecasters suggest Democrats could win their largest House majority since 2009, while Republicans point to a productive two-year record on immigration and taxes.

stories.headline: Suspected Cyber-Attack Hits Supermarket Freezers in Seven European Countries
stories.summary:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit by a suspected cyber-attack that disabled refrigerators and freezers. About 40 Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, along with a smaller number of shops in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Temperatures in some units reportedly climbed as high as 50C (122F).

Sabcobel, the Belgian maker of some of the affected units, said the evaporators were switched to defrost mode, the same method believed used in an incident last month that hit hundreds of French supermarkets. CEO Stephan Moelans called it a cyber-attack and said staff worked through the night to disconnect affected units from the network. He said the units need physical modifications, not just software updates, to close the vulnerability.

Local media reported millions of euros' worth of food was discarded. A Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart said it lost about 100,000 euros of produce. Carrefour said 15 Belgian stores were affected, Colruyt reported five Spar shops hit, and several ICA and Coop stores in Sweden were affected.

No one has been identified as responsible. Belgian and Swedish national cyber-security agencies are monitoring the incident, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it is working with international partners. No incidents have been reported in the UK.

stories.headline: Ryanair Weighs Pay Freeze and Warns of Double-Digit Fare Rises as Iran War Lifts Fuel Costs
stories.summary:
Ryanair said it is considering a temporary wage freeze and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran. The airline expects elevated fuel prices "well into 2027" absent a swift resolution, and forecast its fuel bill will be about 2 billion euros higher in the short term.

CEO Michael O'Leary said fares would rise by double digits across Europe from all airlines in 2027, though he doubted the 20 percent increase he had earlier said was needed would be reached. Pre-tax profit for the six months to September fell 16 percent to 2.4 billion euros, as fuel costs rose 15 percent. About 80 percent of its fuel was hedged.

The pay freeze could begin in April as multi-year labor agreements mature. Unite, which represents Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of any such proposals and expects its multi-year pay deal, which covers next year, to be honoured. Ryanair also plans slower hiring, more use of artificial intelligence in back-office functions, and further winter flight cuts.

O'Leary said capacity cuts would continue into summer 2027 and that short-haul capacity will stay constrained out to the early 2030s, pointing to wider effects of the Gulf conflict on aviation supply.

stories.headline: Uganda Begins Withdrawing Troops From Somalia After Two Decades
stories.summary:
Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades. Acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi said Monday the first group deployed under a bilateral arrangement has returned home and others will follow within days. All forces, including those in the African Union mission, will exit by the end of 2027 in a phased withdrawal.

A first contingent of 109 soldiers reportedly left Mogadishu on Friday after army chief Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced the pullout, writing on X that Uganda was handing security to Somali forces after "20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice." About 4,500 Ugandan troops serve under the AU mission, with roughly 2,000 more deployed bilaterally.

The move follows a meeting in Kampala last week in which Somali President Sheikh Mohamud reportedly sought to persuade President Yoweri Museveni to extend the deployment. Uganda was the first country to deploy under the African Union mission established in 2007 and helped drive al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda affiliate, from Mogadishu and other major towns.

The current AU mission faces uncertain funding as US and UN support winds down, and a 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, raising questions about Somalia's ability to hold ground against the insurgency.

stories.headline: Update: Binance Customers Withdraw $3.6 Billion as Exchange Reopens After Largest Crypto Hack
stories.summary:
Customers withdrew a net $3.6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, as it reopened on Sunday after what is believed to be the largest hack in history. The breach affected $6.3 billion in digital assets and forced the company to suspend all transactions. Binance said it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 06:00 and 15:30 GMT on November 1. It said the net outflow equals just over 2% of the $171 billion in assets it manages, and that withdrawals were stabilizing after an initial spike.

The FBI and other organizations have accused North Korea of responsibility. The attack has been attributed to TraderTraitor, also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange in 2025. On Saturday the FBI published a list of wallet addresses linked to the group and urged industry partners to block transactions involving them. Binance said early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer.

Binance says it has covered about 95% of the stolen assets using its corporate treasury, futures insurance fund and emergency reserves, and that the remainder may take longer to source. It has repeatedly pledged to cover all losses. The hack hit Binance.com, while its US-facing platform said it was unaffected.

Chainalysis, which is working with the firm and governments to recover funds, says the stolen money is still being laundered actively, layered across thousands of addresses and deposits. Withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, have resumed, and other services will return in phases once security checks are finished.

stories.headline: Carney Reports Progress in Trade Talks With Trump; Trump Says Deal 'Concept' Is in Place
stories.summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday he had a constructive conversation with President Donald Trump about a potential trade deal, with negotiators set to work toward an agreement in the coming weeks. Carney said the talks built on recent discussions about a deal that would create jobs, lower costs for families and protect Canada's languages, culture and sovereignty. Hours later, at a rally in Iowa, Trump said, "We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada" and that the sides are "very close."

Trump said the negotiations involve construction of the Keystone XL pipeline and the possibility that U.S. farmers would pay no tariffs on Canadian products, though he acknowledged final details are not settled. The two sides have discussed relief from U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and automobiles, but no specifics have been announced.

The upbeat tone marks a shift from August, when Canada walked away from talks after rejecting U.S. demands that Carney said threatened Canadian sovereignty, French-language protections and the auto industry. Trump then imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods, and Canada retaliated. As recently as Wednesday, Carney said no agreement was possible before Tuesday's midterm elections.

The trade war has become a campaign issue, particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Senate races are closely watched. Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has called for an end to the tariff dispute. Negotiators are expected to work over the coming weeks, and any agreement would need its details confirmed by both governments.

stories.headline: Supreme Court to Hear Colorado Preschool Case Pitting Religious Liberty Against LGBTQ Rights
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court is set to hear arguments Tuesday on whether Colorado can require preschools that receive public funds to admit the children of same-sex couples. The case is the latest to place religious liberty and LGBTQ rights in tension on the court's docket. It arrives as the nation prepares for midterm elections.

During discussion of the case, one comment reflecting the religious-liberty side held that "it seems like there's short shrift being given to religious liberty in the state of Colorado." Supporters of Colorado's requirement argue that programs taking public dollars must follow nondiscrimination rules and serve all families equally.

The decision will affect how states may condition public funding on nondiscrimination policies for religious institutions. Separately, national groups are spending money in battleground judicial races, hoping to build liberal majorities on state courts within two years. A ruling is expected later in the court's term.

stories.headline: Xi Hosts Oman's Sultan, Offers Help on Hormuz Shipping Amid Fallout From US-Iran War
stories.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping offered to help address challenges in the Middle East and seek safe passage for ships through the Strait of Hormuz during an unprecedented visit to China by Oman's sultan. Both countries are grappling with the fallout from the US war with Iran.

The Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and costly for shipping, despite US claims that it is open. Oman, which borders the strait, has long served as a diplomatic intermediary in the region, and China is a major buyer of Gulf energy.

The visit underscores Beijing's interest in a larger role in Gulf diplomacy while the waterway's disruption raises costs worldwide. Airlines such as Ryanair have already cited surging fuel prices tied to the conflict. No specific agreements on shipping were detailed in the initial report.
